newsitem.title: USA: Next CRP signup in Oct or Nov, USDA aide says.
newsitem.headline: Next CRP signup in Oct or Nov, USDA aide says.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department will hold the next enrollment of crop acreage into the Conservation Reserve Program sometime in October or November, a key aide said Thursday.

Although U.S. wheat growers have requested the USDA hold the next signup in August, the expected work load at county offices makes it impractical to hold another sign-up before early fall, said Parks Shackleford, deputy assistant administrator of USDA's Farm Service Agency.

On Wednesday, the House Appropriations Committee passed a fiscal 1998 spending bill that, among other things, would eliminate funding for the jobs held by Shackleford and FSA Deputy Administrator Richard Newman.

On nearly straight party-line vote, the Republican-controlled panel took the action at the request of Rep. George Nethercutt, a Washington Republican, who was angry about his state's poor showing in the spring CRP signup.
Nethercutt made Shackleford and Newman the object of his wrath because he said they rejected a plan submitted by state USDA officials for reevaluating Washington state bids.
The USDA accepted only about 20 percent of the acres offered by Washington farmers during the spring signup, compared to about 80 percent in neighboring Oregon and Idaho.

Shackleford declined to comment on the committee's action. However, he repeated that USDA may revamp its air quality criteria for CRP enrollment for the next CRP signup to give greater weight to blowing dust as a result of volcanic ash in Washington soils.
USDA officials have also said expiring CRP acreage accepted in the next signup will be allowed to immediately reenter the program.
That means some land due to come out of the CRP on September 30, could reenter early in 1997 and miss only a few month's CRP payments.
That will likely discourage some Washington farmers whose CRP bids were narrowly rejected to keep their expiring CRP land out of crop production this fall, Shackleford said.
But other land "that isn't as close" may go back into production, he said.
Despite the appropriation committee's action, Shackleford said he did not expect that USDA to reevaluate all of Washington's bid from the spring signup.
However, it will continue to review individual appeals in Washington and in other states, he said.
